title: Inter-Task Communication: FreeRTOS Queues, Direct-to-Task Notifications & Event Groups
goal: Communicate safely between concurrent tasks: master FreeRTOS communication primitives. Understand copy-by-value queue memory isolation, Direct-to-Task notifications (zero-RAM overhead), multi-event bitmask synchronization groups, and interrupt-safe deferred processing via xQueueSendFromISR.
recap: Yesterday, we conquered task synchronization, mutexes, and priority inheritance. Today, we master data transport between tasks: thread-safe queues, zero-overhead direct notifications, and interrupt-to-task pipelines.

parts.title: FreeRTOS Queues: Copy-by-Value Memory Isolation Invariant & Thread-Safe Ring Buffers
say: In multi-tasking systems, tasks must pass data packets to each other without corrupting memory or introducing race conditions.
The primary communication mechanism in FreeRTOS is the Queue (`QueueHandle_t`).
Crucial Invariant: FreeRTOS queues operate strictly by COPY-BY-VALUE, not copy-by-reference.

When a task sends an item via `xQueueSend()`, the kernel copies the byte payload directly into its private internal ring buffer; when the receiving task calls `xQueueReceive()`, the bytes are copied into the receiver's local variable.
Because data is copied by value, the sending task can immediately overwrite, re-use, or exit the function that created the original variable with 100% safety.
Copy-by-value completely eliminates dangling pointers, memory leaks, and multi-threaded race conditions.
parts.example: Mailing a physical letter: you photocopy your document and drop the paper copy in the mailbox (queue); you can shred or rewrite your original draft on your desk, and the recipient still gets the exact copy you mailed.
parts.output:
[QUEUE SEND] Item copied into kernel storage (Queue Fill: 1/4)
[QUEUE RECEIVE] Item copied out of kernel storage (Remaining: 0)
Received Sensor Reading: Temp = 28 C (Verified uncorrupted!)

codeNotes.note: storage[head] = item executes byte-for-byte copy into kernel buffer
Modifying localData does not affect the data already queued in kernel memory
Receiver receives original uncorrupted 28 C temperature payload

parts.tryIt: Demonstrate the fatal bug of passing pointers to stack-allocated variables through queues.

check.question: Why does FreeRTOS use Copy-by-Value rather than Copy-by-Reference for queue messages?
options: To guarantee memory isolation so the sender can safely modify or discard its local variable without corrupting the receiver
Because pointers are not supported in embedded C
To reduce the size of the microcontroller Flash memory
Because the ARM processor does not support RAM
check.why: Copy-by-value ensures complete memory decoupling: tasks do not share pointers, preventing race conditions and dangling pointer bugs.

parts.title: Passing Complex Data Without Corruption: Senders, Receivers & Bounded Timeout Blocking
say: FreeRTOS queues provide built-in real-time blocking: tasks specify a timeout in ticks (`TicksToWait`).
If a task attempts to receive from an empty queue (`xQueueReceive`), it enters the BLOCKED state and consumes 0% CPU cycles until data arrives or the timeout expires.
If a task attempts to send to a full queue (`xQueueSend`), it blocks until another task reads a packet, creating automatic backpressure and rate limiting.
For large payloads (such as a 10KB display framebuffer or camera image), copying 10KB by value through a queue would be inefficient.
In such cases, the established pattern is Queue of Pointers: software allocates a static or pool buffer, and sends the 4-byte pointer through the queue.
Invariant: When passing pointers through queues, strict ownership transfer must be maintained: the sender must never touch the buffer after sending until the receiver explicitly hands it back.
parts.example: Passing a heavy cargo shipping container: you don't mail the container itself through the postal system; you mail the paper bill of lading (the pointer) that authorizes the recipient to take ownership of the container at the shipping dock.
parts.output:
[QUEUE POINTER] Passed pointer to Frame #101 (Only 4 bytes copied across queue!)
[QUEUE POINTER] Receiver took ownership of Frame #101
Received Frame ID: 101 (Zero-copy transfer complete!)

codeNotes.note: Passes 4-byte memory pointer through queue instead of copying 1024-byte payload
Transfers exclusive buffer ownership to receiver task
Demonstrates high-performance zero-copy buffer passing for large payloads

parts.tryIt: Explain why sending pointers to dynamically allocated malloc buffers requires strict ownership discipline to prevent memory leaks.

check.question: When is it appropriate to pass pointers through a FreeRTOS queue rather than copying values directly?
options: When transmitting large payloads (e.g. image frames, network packets) where copying entire structures would waste CPU cycles and RAM
Only when the microcontroller has no stack
When all tasks have identical priorities
Never, pointers are illegal in FreeRTOS
check.why: For large structures, copying only the 32-bit pointer preserves memory bandwidth and CPU cycles, provided ownership transfer rules are strictly followed.

parts.title: Direct-to-Task Notifications: Zero-RAM Overhead & 45% Faster Context Swaps
say: While FreeRTOS queues and semaphores are versatile, every queue requires an allocated `Queue_t` control structure in SRAM (approx 80–120 bytes of RAM).
To achieve ultra-lightweight communication, FreeRTOS introduced Direct-to-Task Notifications (`xTaskNotify` / `ulTaskNotifyTake`).
Every Task Control Block (`TCB_t`) natively includes an embedded 32-bit notification value and a notification state at ZERO additional RAM cost.
A task or ISR can send an event directly to a target task using its task handle.
Task notifications can emulate binary semaphores (unblocking a waiting task), counting semaphores, or lightweight mailbox registers.
Benchmark measurements prove that Direct-to-Task Notifications execute up to 45% faster than standard binary semaphores and consume exactly 0 bytes of dynamic heap memory.
parts.example: Instead of building a community mailbox at the end of the road (creating a queue), the mail carrier knocks directly on your front door and hands you the package.
parts.output:
[NOTIFY BLOCKED] Task blocked waiting for direct notification...
[NOTIFY GIVE] Sent direct event to task! (Value = 1)
  -> [UNBLOCKED] Target task immediately unblocked!
[NOTIFY TAKE] Direct notification consumed (Value decremented to 0)

codeNotes.note: Notification value resides directly inside target task's TCB structure
notifyGive unblocks target task directly without intermediate queue objects
Demonstrates 0-RAM overhead synchronization executing 45% faster than semaphores

parts.tryIt: Configure notificationValue as a bitmask where different bits represent different hardware events.

check.question: What is the primary architectural advantage of FreeRTOS Direct-to-Task Notifications over binary semaphores?
options: They require exactly 0 bytes of additional RAM (built directly into the TCB) and execute up to 45% faster
They can transmit infinite amounts of data
They do not require a CPU clock
They work across different circuit boards
check.why: Task notifications store the notification value directly within the existing TCB, eliminating dynamic memory allocation and reducing scheduler traversal overhead.

parts.title: Multi-Condition Synchronization: Event Groups, Synchronization Bits & Rendezvous Barriers
say: What happens when a task needs to wait for multiple independent events to occur simultaneously (e.g., 'wait until Wi-Fi is connected AND GPS has a 3D fix AND Battery is above 20%')?
Doing this with multiple queues or semaphores results in complex nested blocking and race conditions.
The solution is FreeRTOS Event Groups (`EventGroupHandle_t`).
An Event Group maintains a 24-bit bitmask of event flags.
Tasks can wait for any combination of bits using `xEventGroupWaitBits()`.
The function supports `xWaitForAllBits = pdTRUE` (logical AND: unblock only when ALL requested bits are set) or `pdFALSE` (logical OR: unblock when ANY bit is set).
Event groups also provide the `xEventGroupSync()` rendezvous barrier: multiple concurrent tasks synchronize at a barrier and release simultaneously.
parts.example: A rocket launch sequence: the launch director's console has 3 green lights: Propulsion Ready (Bit 0), Guidance Ready (Bit 1), and Weather Go (Bit 2); the countdown only triggers when all three lights are lit simultaneously.
parts.output:
[EVENT GROUP] Set bits 0x1 -> Active Mask: 0x1
[EVENT GROUP] Set bits 0x2 -> Active Mask: 0x3
[EVENT WAIT] Waiting for 0x7 (Mode: AND (ALL))
  -> [BLOCKED] Condition not met. Task blocks.
[EVENT GROUP] Set bits 0x4 -> Active Mask: 0x7
[EVENT WAIT] Waiting for 0x7 (Mode: AND (ALL))
  -> [BARRIER PASSED] All requested event bits asserted!

codeNotes.note: Maintains 24-bit event bitmask accessible by all concurrent tasks and ISRs
Evaluates logical AND condition (waitForAll=true) requiring all bits to match
Unblocks launch task only when Wi-Fi, GPS, and sensors are simultaneously ready

parts.tryIt: Set waitForAll to false and demonstrate that the task unblocks as soon as the first bit (Wi-Fi) is set.

check.question: How do FreeRTOS Event Groups allow a task to wait for multiple independent system events to complete?
options: By evaluating an atomic 24-bit bitmask with logical AND (all bits) or logical OR (any bit) matching options
By polling each event in an infinite while loop
By creating 24 separate threads
By turning off the CPU cache
check.why: Event groups allow tasks to block on a 24-bit bitmask, unblocking atomically when all specified bits or any specified bit is set by tasks or ISRs.

parts.title: From ISR to Task: xQueueSendFromISR, portYIELD_FROM_ISR & Deferred Processing
say: A critical rule of real-time operating systems is: NEVER call standard RTOS API functions (`xQueueSend`, `xSemaphoreTake`) inside an Interrupt Service Routine.
Standard API functions can block; an interrupt service routine must NEVER enter a blocked state.
FreeRTOS provides dedicated ISR-safe functions ending with `FromISR` (such as `xQueueSendFromISR`, `xSemaphoreGiveFromISR`).
These functions accept a pointer argument: `BaseType_t *pxHigherPriorityTaskWoken`.
If sending an item to a queue causes a higher-priority task to unblock, the kernel sets `*pxHigherPriorityTaskWoken = pdTRUE`.

Before exiting the ISR, firmware invokes `portYIELD_FROM_ISR(xHigherPriorityTaskWoken)`: if true, the hardware asserts the PendSV bit, ensuring the CPU context-switches directly into the unblocked high-priority task the microsecond the ISR exits.
parts.example: A fast delivery driver dropping a package on the porch: the driver doesn't wait inside your house; they ring the doorbell (set higher priority task woken) and leave immediately; you walk to the door and open the package outside of interrupt context.
parts.output:
[HARDWARE UART ISR] Byte received: 0xaa
  -> xQueueSendFromISR: Message queued safely without blocking
  -> portYIELD_FROM_ISR(pdTRUE): PendSV bit set! Deferred switch armed.
[PENDSV HANDLER] Immediate switch to high-priority ParserTask!
  -> [PARSER TASK] Processed payload: 0xaa

codeNotes.note: xQueueSendFromISR never blocks and sets higherPriorityTaskWoken if unblocking occurs
portYIELD_FROM_ISR arms PendSV to trigger immediate task switch on ISR exit
High-priority parser task executes immediately after ISR returns with zero latency

parts.tryIt: Explain why calling a blocking xQueueSend() inside an ISR triggers a fatal kernel assertion.

check.question: What is the purpose of the portYIELD_FROM_ISR() macro inside an interrupt service routine?
options: It triggers an immediate context switch to the unblocked task via PendSV if a higher-priority task was woken by the ISR
It pauses all hardware timers
It reboots the microcontroller
It disables the global interrupt controller
check.why: portYIELD_FROM_ISR requests a context switch if pxHigherPriorityTaskWoken is true, ensuring the newly unblocked task runs immediately as the ISR exits.

summary: FreeRTOS queues enforce copy-by-value memory isolation, eliminating multi-threaded race conditions and dangling pointer bugs.
Queues of pointers provide zero-copy high-performance transport for large buffers (display, network) through strict ownership transfer.
Direct-to-Task Notifications embed an event value inside the TCB, executing up to 45% faster than semaphores with 0 bytes of dynamic RAM.
Event Groups evaluate 24-bit bitmasks with logical AND/OR matching, synchronizing multiple concurrent conditions and rendezvous barriers.
FromISR API functions never block, and portYIELD_FROM_ISR ensures newly unblocked high-priority tasks run the instant the hardware ISR returns.

projectStep.title: Construct an Event-Driven Multi-Sensor FreeRTOS Pipeline with Queue Backpressure
steps: Implement a thread-safe copy-by-value FreeRTOS queue transferring structured telemetry packets.
Configure bounded timeout blocking on sender and receiver to implement automatic flow control backpressure.
Integrate Direct-to-Task notifications for lightweight task signaling with zero dynamic memory allocation.
Implement an Event Group rendezvous barrier synchronizing system startup across Wi-Fi, GPS, and sensors.
Construct an interrupt-safe deferred processing pipeline using xQueueSendFromISR and portYIELD_FROM_ISR.
